opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the big thing is that every time you hard-code a workflow around the model, you're basically baking in your own assumptions about how the problem should be solved, and those assumptions tend to age really badly. When we were working on SWE-bench, we tried a lot of the more elaborate setups people were using: fixed pipelines where you first localize the bug, then write a reproduction, then edit, then test, each as a separate stage. And what we found was that if you just give Claude a small set of good tools, like a bash tool and a file editing tool, and let it loop, calling tools until it decides it's done, it does as well or better, and it's way more flexible.

Part of the reason is that real problems don't follow a script. Sometimes the bug is obvious and you should just fix it. Sometimes you need to go explore the repo for a while, or write a test, discover your hypothesis was wrong, and backtrack. A rigid pipeline either forces unnecessary steps or doesn't allow the ones you actually need. The model is often better at deciding what to do next than whatever flowchart I'd draw in advance.

The other piece is that it scales with model improvements. If your scaffolding is thin, then when a smarter model comes out, you just drop it in and you get the gains for free. If you've built a ton of clever structure to compensate for the weaknesses of last year's model, that structure often becomes a ceiling. So my philosophy is to put the effort into the things that really matter: designing the tools well, writing clear tool descriptions, making error messages informative, thinking about the agent-computer interface the way you'd think about a UI for a human. Then get out of the way and let the model drive.

It's not that structure is never useful. For narrow, well-defined, high-volume tasks, a fixed workflow can be cheaper and more predictable. But for open-ended work like coding, I'd much rather start minimal and only add complexity when I see a specific failure that justifies it.

r001.rationale: The response says thin scaffolding lets smarter models gain from improvements, while elaborate structure can become a ceiling.

r002.rationale: It describes Claude exploring, revising a wrong hypothesis, and backtracking, but does not identify Claude Sonnet 3.5 as the model with this capability.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, a lot of it comes from watching what happens when you do the opposite. When we were building our early agents, the instinct was always to scaffold everything. You write this big orchestration layer, you decide the plan up front, you break the task into steps, you route between sub-agents, you add retries and guardrails at every junction. And it feels productive, because you're writing a lot of code. But what you're really doing is baking your own assumptions about how the task should be solved into the system, and those assumptions are usually worse than what the model would have come up with on its own.

The thing that kept happening is that the model got better, and all that scaffolding turned into a ceiling instead of a floor. Every decision we'd hardcoded was a place where we were preventing the model from doing something smarter. So we'd ship a new model, and the agent would barely improve, because the agent wasn't really the model, it was our framework with the model stuck inside it.

So the version we landed on is almost embarrassingly simple. You give Claude a clear goal, you give it a good set of tools, and you let it run in a loop: think, call a tool, look at the result, decide what to do next, and keep going until it decides it's done. That's basically it. The intelligence lives in the model, not in the harness.

And the reason that works is that the hard part of agentic work isn't the plumbing, it's the judgment. Knowing when to read one more file, when to run the tests again, when to stop and ask the user, when the thing you just saw means your original plan was wrong. Those are exactly the decisions a static framework is bad at and a model is increasingly good at. If you force the model through a fixed sequence, you lose all of that.

There's also a practical thing, which is that a minimal loop is much easier to debug. When something goes wrong, you can read the transcript and see exactly what the model saw and why it did what it did. With a heavy framework, you spend half your time figuring out whether the failure was the model's fault or your orchestration's fault.

That doesn't mean zero structure. We care a lot about the tools themselves, their descriptions, what they return, making errors informative so the model can recover. And we spend real effort on the environment and on good stopping conditions. But that effort goes into making the model's world legible, not into telling the model what to do. The bet is that models keep getting better at being agents, and we want to be positioned so that every improvement shows up directly, rather than being absorbed by a framework that was designed around last year's limitations.

r001.rationale: It says that as models improve, hardcoded scaffolding becomes a ceiling that prevents them from making better decisions.

r002.rationale: It mentions that the model can recover from informative tool errors, but does not state that Claude Sonnet 3.5 responds to failed attempts by trying different approaches.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that you want to let the model do what it’s good at: figure out what to do next based on what it just learned. If you hard-code a workflow, you’re making a bunch of assumptions up front about what the task is going to require. And then the agent encounters something you didn’t anticipate, and it needs to go sideways or take another step, but your framework doesn’t allow that.

So I prefer a simple loop: give Claude the goal and the tools, let it take an action, show it the result, and let it decide what comes next. You still need clear boundaries and good tool interfaces. But you don’t need to prescribe every intermediate step. And as the model improves, that simple loop can benefit directly, without you having to redesign a bunch of orchestration around it.

r001.rationale: The response says models should choose their own next steps, that intermediate steps need not be prescribed, and that an improving model can benefit from a simple loop without redesigned orchestration. This communicates reduced reliance on external scaffolding as models improve.

r002.rationale: It discusses handling unanticipated needs by taking another step, but does not state that Claude Sonnet 3.5 can respond to failed attempts by trying different approaches.

sol-6.1.text:
The main reason is that you want to take advantage of the model’s judgment. If you hard-code a workflow—first search, then read three files, then write some code—you’re making a lot of assumptions about what the task will need. Sometimes the right next step is another search. Sometimes it’s running a test. Sometimes it’s asking the user a question.

So I prefer a simple loop: give Claude a goal and a set of tools, let it take an action, show it the result, and let it decide what to do next. That gives it room to recover when something fails or follow up on something unexpected.

You still need clear tool definitions, useful feedback, and boundaries around what it can do. But the framework’s job is to support that loop. The less task-specific logic you bake into the orchestration, the more you can benefit as the model gets better.

r001.rationale: It favors less task-specific orchestration and says that approach benefits as models improve, but does not clearly state that more capable models need less externally imposed scaffolding.

r002.rationale: It says Claude can recover when something fails and gives examples of different next steps, but does not identify Claude Sonnet 3.5 as having that capability.
